changelog/v0.24.6.0.md:23:- **Existing references follow the move.** References that pointed to the router in `SKILL.md` now point to `ROUTER.md` §3; the testing playbooks and feature catalog entries still cite the older target.
changelog/v0.19.0.0.md:22:`obsidian-local-rest-api` was the one enabled vault plugin without a dedicated reference folder. feature-catalog/plugins/health-md.md:18:Health.md Visualizations (repo `codybontecou/health-md-visualizations`, installed v2.1.0 in every vault by Phase 11) renders Apple Health and Android Health exports from plain data files in a vault folder (default `Health/`). The mode operates the **data files**, never the chart UI. Formats: JSON (`healthmd.health_data` daily schema through v8), CSV, Markdown frontmatter (Bases-style), Obsidian Bases; roll-ups are `healthmd.rollup_summary` v9. Compatibility profiles: Apple current export daily v8 / roll-up v9 (whether installed plugin v2.1.0 reads v8/v9 is VERIFY — historically v0–v7), Android frozen v4, and Android analytical v5 — format names are shared, but version and semantic differences stay explicit. Chart coverage is shared across platforms for common activity, heart, respiratory/vitals, sleep, mobility, workout, body, nutrition, and hearing fields; Mood/State of Mind and HealthKit-style medication events are iOS-only; Android walking symmetry is partial and Android Stand can use an explicit steps-derived proxy when `standHours` is missing. Roll-ups live under `Health/Rollups/`; `_healthmd_data_dictionary.json` holds canonical metric ids/units. The plugin watches the folder and refreshes its cache on file changes. A `health-viz` block's `type` must be a registered renderer (43 documented across 18 categories — catalog in `references/plugins/health-md/health-md.md` §4). Beyond the plugin, the companion app (`healthmd.app`) can merge metrics into Obsidian daily-note frontmatter and ships a `healthmd` CLI and a `healthmd-mcp` MCP server (21 tools reading iPhone HealthKit via a Mac loopback) — separate from this plugin; see `references/plugins/health-md/health-md.md` §7.

references/troubleshooting.md:265:4. Re-test with the `curl` command in §6.
references/mcp-tools.md:34:- Routing a request to MCP (not the CLI) because a live app + Local REST API is available — see the router in `../ROUTER.md` §3 MACHINE ROUTER
references/mcp-tools.md:90:> The router in `../ROUTER.md` §3 MACHINE ROUTER picks between them by whether a live app/token is available: app present → MCP; headless → CLI.
references/plugins/health-md/health-md.md:139:- **A rendered chart is not evidence** (see §5): with a missing/empty data folder the plugin shows bundled example data.
references/obsidian-cli-commands.md:145:The official `obsidian` CLI needs an **already-running** app and does not start one. Do not route a file-shaped task to it. Reach for it only when the result requires the live app (§9), and before depending on it run the preflight `obsidian version` and check its output looks like a version — exit 0 means the binary is registered and the app is up. Once the app is running the CLI **exits 0 on failure**, so check its stdout for a leading `Error:` rather than `$?`. Full contract: [`official-cli-agent-usage.md`](official-cli-agent-usage.md).
references/obsidian-cli-commands.md:195:| `notesmd-cli delete <note>` | Delete a note | Destructive — see agent invariants (§4) |
references/obsidian-cli-commands.md:220:> **Headless note:** every subcommand above operates on the vault **filesystem** and needs **no running Obsidian app**. This is what makes `notesmd-cli` safe for servers, CI, and unattended agent runs. Behavior that requires the live app (rendering, plugin execution, UI focus) is out of scope for `notesmd-cli` — use the official `obsidian` CLI (§9) for that.
references/plugins/plugin-operation-logic.md:110:These references are loaded on demand by the `mcp-obsidian` router in [`ROUTER.md` §3](../../ROUTER.md#3-machine-router) when a request mentions health data or icon rules. See `assets/workflows.md` for end-to-end procedures.
references/plugins/installed-plugins.md:57:These plugins persist their state as markdown, frontmatter, or a structured file, so the file-layer operating model in `plugin-operation-logic.md` applies to them exactly as it applies in §2.
references/plugins/installed-plugins.md:107:3. Add or remove its row in §2 (documented file-layer, with a `references/plugins/<name>/` tree), §3 (file-layer whose dedicated docs were removed), or §4 (UI/automatic, never documented).
references/plugins/installed-plugins.md:108:4. Keep the total in §1 in step with the row count (2 promoted + 13 undocumented + 9 UI/automatic = 24).
references/plugins/installed-plugins.md:110:A plugin belongs in §2 only if the mode ships a four-file reference tree for it under `references/plugins/<name>/`. A file-layer plugin without that tree belongs in §3, and a plugin whose configuration is display preferences, URLs, or automatic behavior belongs in §4.
references/official-cli-agent-usage.md:90:> Obsidian's own documentation at `https://obsidian.md/help/cli` states that "the first command you run launches Obsidian". The binary contradicts that. See §9.
references/official-cli-agent-usage.md:178:> **Agent default stays `notesmd-cli`.** It has no app dependency and no exit-code trap. Escalate to the official CLI when the result requires the live app, and preflight per §2 before depending on it.
references/official-cli-agent-usage.md:226:| `create` | `name=` `path=` `content=` `template=` `overwrite` `open` `newtab` | Prints `Created: <name>.md`. **See §7 on collisions.** |
references/official-cli-agent-usage.md:234:| `eval` | `code=` | Runs JavaScript inside the app and prints `=> <result>`. **See §7.** |
references/official-cli-agent-usage.md:334:| "If Obsidian isn't running, the first command you run launches Obsidian." | Prints `The CLI is unable to find Obsidian...` to stderr, exits 1, and does **not** launch the app. | Any workflow relying on auto-launch fails on a cold machine. Launch it explicitly per §2. |
references/plugins/health-md/troubleshooting.md:41:| Platform-specific surface missing | iOS-only feature on Android, or a known Android gap (see §3) |
references/plugins/health-md/troubleshooting.md:78:| Render block with wrong type or metric | Check `type` against the renderer catalog ([`health-md.md`](health-md.md) §4) and copy a known-good block from the vault; verify the renderer and metric first |
references/plugins/health-md/workflows.md:72:- `type` is required and must name a registered renderer — pick from the renderer catalog in [`health-md.md`](health-md.md) §4 (43 documented types; the installed build may expose a subset, and iOS-only types render nothing on Android data). Common optional keys: `width`, `height`, inclusive `from`/`to`, `last`, `clickAction`.
references/plugins/health-md/workflows.md:96:The Health.md app can merge metrics into Obsidian daily-note frontmatter and inject app-managed markdown sections (HTML-comment-wrapped) on every export. Treat those managed frontmatter keys and comment-wrapped sections as **app-owned**: read them, but never hand-edit inside them — the next export overwrites the edit. Author your own content outside the managed blocks. See [`health-md.md`](health-md.md) §7 for the target-folder and filename-placeholder conventions.

16: # Reference — Plugin operation logic (file-layer model)
17: 
18: The `mcp-obsidian` mode operates Obsidian community plugins by editing the data they read, never by driving their UI. This is the connective principle that makes the per-plugin references usable and the pattern to extend to any future plugin.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: `plugin-operation-logic.md` ships in the `mcp-obsidian` mode at `references/plugins/` and defines one operating model for every plugin the mode covers: locate the plugin's persisted data, edit the data directly, and let the app re-render. The surviving per-plugin and theme references (`health-md`, `iconic`, `minimal`) apply this model to their specific file shapes; this document is the general contract.
27: 
28: ### When to Use
29: 
30: - Any request that changes what a plugin shows or computes (icons, health charts, theme appearance).
31: - Deciding whether a plugin capability is reachable headlessly before promising it to the operator.
32: - Extending the mode to a plugin not yet covered by a per-plugin reference.
33: 
34: ### Core Principle
35: 
36: > **Operate a plugin's features by editing the DATA the plugin reads — not by driving the plugin's UI.**
37: 
38: The mode has no headless UI bridge, so command-palette actions and in-app buttons are out of reach. Almost every plugin persists its state as text/JSON in the vault, and *that* is directly operable.
39: 
40: ### Prerequisites
41: 
42: - Per-plugin identity and schema: `references/plugins/plugin-operation-logic.md` siblings under `references/plugins/{plugin}/`.
43: - End-to-end procedures: `assets/workflows.md`.
44: - File-layer scenarios: `manual-testing-playbook/plugin-tie-ins/`.
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## 2. WHERE PLUGINS KEEP THEIR DATA
49: 
50: For any plugin, locate its data by checking, in order:
51: 
52: 1. A **document convention** — a dedicated file extension, a fenced code-block language (e.g. a `health-viz` render block), or a frontmatter key.
53: 2. A **plain-text ledger/sidecar** the plugin renders (e.g. a structured data file at a configured path).
54: 3. **Plugin settings/state** at `<vault>/.obsidian/plugins/{plugin-id}/data.json`.
55: 4. **Vault-level plugin state** — `community-plugins.json` (enabled ids), `app.json`, `appearance.json`.
56: 
57: **Validation**: `plugin_data_located` — the exact file (not a folder) that drives the requested behavior is named, read, and its schema matched before any mutation.
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## 3. THE THREE ARTIFACTS — DATA MAP
62: 
63: | Artifact | Data the AI edits | Operation |
64: |--------|-------------------|-----------|
65: | `health-md` | Apple + Android Health export files in the data folder (default `Health/`), JSON/CSV/Markdown/Bases | `health-viz` render blocks; create/append/patch data files; verify real folder + authentic source (bundled mock-data fallback renders on empty folder); NEVER fabricate data |
66: | `iconic` | `.obsidian/plugins/iconic/data.json` (rulebook + settings) | merge rules/toggles with backup-before-write; preserve unrelated keys; rendering is in-app |
67: | `minimal` | theme: `.obsidian/themes/Minimal/theme.css` + `appearance.json` `cssTheme` key | verify install/activation; propose snippet-based tweaks (`.obsidian/snippets/`); never edit `theme.css` in a real vault |
68: 
69: **Validation**: `plugin_data_map_applied` — the row above names the exact data artifact and the exact mutation discipline before the agent edits anything.
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 4. WHAT THE FILE LAYER CAN AND CANNOT DO
74: 
75: ### CAN (file writes fully suffice)
76: 
77: - Create/append/patch a plugin's data document (a transaction, a table row, a note).
78: - Enable a plugin (edit `community-plugins.json`).
79: - Query/aggregate over the data (the AI computes; it does not need the plugin's UI compute).
80: 
81: ### CANNOT (needs the app / a reload)
82: 
83: - Invoke command-palette commands or click ribbon icons.
84: - Force in-app computations that only run on render (e.g. a Health.md `health-viz` render block draws its chart when the note is opened — the AI writes the block; Obsidian renders it).
85: - Guarantee a live view refreshes without the user reloading the note/pane.
86: 
87: **Note:** the file-layer model covers everything the plugin persists. If a capability is not reachable through a persisted artifact, it is out of reach headlessly.
88: 
89: **Out of scope:** driving the plugin UI, in-app computation, and anything that only exists in the running renderer.
90: 
91: ### Discipline
92: 
93: Write the data, then tell the user (or a smoke step) to open/reload the relevant note so the plugin re-renders. Append is safest; in-place patches must preserve the plugin's exact schema or the file won't render.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ## 5. EXTENDING TO A NEW PLUGIN
98: 
99: 1. Fetch the plugin's README + manifest; record repo id, author, data convention.
100: 2. Generate one real artifact in-app, then **match its on-disk shape** (this removes schema guesswork).
101: 3. Write a per-plugin reference mirroring `iconic.md` / `health-md.md`: identity → what it does → data model → settings → file-layer recipes → gotchas/VERIFY → sources.
102: 4. Add a row to the plugin data map above and an example asset.
103: 
104: **Validation**: `plugin_reference_complete` — a real artifact's on-disk shape was matched, the per-plugin reference exists, and the data map row plus asset landed.
105: 
106: ---
107: 
108: ## 6. RELATION TO THE MODE
109: 
110: These references are loaded on demand by the `mcp-obsidian` router in [`ROUTER.md` §3](../../ROUTER.md#3-machine-router) when a request mentions health data or icon rules. See `assets/workflows.md` for end-to-end procedures.

18: # Installed Obsidian Plugins Roster (`installed-plugins`)
19: 
20: This is the single source of truth for **every community plugin enabled in the operator's vault** — including the ones that carry no dedicated integration reference. It answers three questions at a glance: what is installed, what each plugin is for, and where (if anywhere) the AI-usable integration docs live.
21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: Keep the vault's plugin inventory and its documentation status in one place, so an install, enablement, or removal has one place to reconcile.
27: 
28: ### When to Use
29: 
30: - A request names an Obsidian plugin and you need its id, version, or repository.
31: - Checking whether a plugin still has a dedicated reference tree.
32: - Reconciling the roster after an install, enablement, or removal.
33: 
34: The vault has **24 community plugins** enabled (`.obsidian/community-plugins.json`). They split into three operating classes, and the counts add up: **2 documented + 13 undocumented file-layer + 9 UI/automatic = 24**.
35: 
36: - **Documented file-layer plugins (2)** — persist their state as markdown, frontmatter, or a structured file, and the mode documents them at the file layer: each has a dedicated four-file integration reference tree under `references/plugins/<name>/` plus a `feature-catalog/plugins/<name>.md` entry. Only these two carry dedicated docs.
37: - **Undocumented file-layer plugins (13)** — persist state an AI edits at the file layer just as directly, but their dedicated reference trees were removed from this skill. They stay installed and operationally supported; the mode reaches them by locating and editing their on-disk data, with no per-plugin reference to follow.
38: - **UI / automatic plugins (9)** — change the editor UI or apply automatic behavior with no vault syntax or data model an AI authors against. These are installed and listed here for completeness but carry **no dedicated integration docs** — there is nothing for an AI to author against.
39: 
40: Ground-truth identity (id, version, `minAppVersion`) always comes from each plugin's on-disk `manifest.json` under `.obsidian/plugins/<manifest.id>/`. The operator's Obsidian app is **1.13.4**, which clears every plugin's minimum-version floor (the highest here is 1.13.1).

53: - **Matching:** rules match by file extension or folder name; per-item overrides exist for individual icons.

59: 
60: | Layer | Path / artifact | Operable by AI |
61: |---|---|---|
62: | Rulebook + settings | `.obsidian/plugins/iconic/data.json` | **Yes** — toggles, colors, `fileRules`/`folderRules`, per-item icon maps |
63: | Enablement | `.obsidian/community-plugins.json` | Yes (already enabled in all vaults) |
64: | In-app icon picking | — | **No** — out of reach headlessly; edit rules instead |
65: 
66: ### Rulebook assets
67: 
68: | Asset | Contents | Use |
69: | --- | --- | --- |
70: | `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.full.json` | **Complete** automatic-rule payload: all 21 `fileRules` + 11 `folderRules` | Canonical copy/merge payload — the only authoritative full rule content |
71: | `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.full.md` | Template-conformant usage guide: rule-class coverage + merge contract | Usage companion for the payload; never a copy/merge source |
72: | `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.example.json` | Compact schema sample (2 file + 1 folder rules) | Schema reference only |
73: 
74: - The full asset contains **only the two mergeable rule arrays** — no `data.json` settings, no `dialogState`, no per-item override maps.
75: - It is **never a whole-`data.json` replacement**: merge it by stable rule `id` into a freshly-read vault `data.json` (update matching ids, append missing ids), preserving unrelated settings and user overrides.

80: 
81: ```json
82: {
83:   "id": "FE8l6",
84:   "name": "Canvas boards",
85:   "icon": "lucide-layout-template",
86:   "color": "#8b5cf6",
87:   "match": "any",
88:   "conditions": [
89:     { "source": "extension", "operator": "is", "value": "canvas" }
90:   ],
91:   "enabled": true
92: }
93: ```
94: 
95: - `source`: `extension` (file rules) or `name` (folder rules).
96: - `operator`: `is` / `contains` (per the live vault rulebook).
97: - `match`: `any` (any condition matches) — `all` is supported by the schema.
98: - `icon`: `lucide-*` names; `color`: hex.

103: 
104: - **Backup before every write.** Take a `.bak` copy of `data.json` before merging (the bundle's `merge_rules.py` pattern: backup → merge → write).
105: - **Merge, never replace.** Preserve every setting and rule not being changed; user-customized rules stay untouched.
106: - **Full asset ≠ full `data.json`.** The canonical rule asset carries only the two rule arrays; applying it never touches settings, `dialogState`, or per-item overrides.
107: - **Never downgrade the plugin.** Only the rulebook is (re)applied.
108: - **Re-read `data.json` before operating** — the user may have changed icons in-app since the last read.
109: - Render confirmation needs an in-app reload; the file-layer claim is verified by JSON round-trip only.

58: ## 4. FILE-LAYER SURFACE (WHAT THE AI EDITS)
59: 
60: | Layer | Path / artifact | Operable by AI |
61: |---|---|---|
62: | Rulebook + settings | `.obsidian/plugins/iconic/data.json` | **Yes** — toggles, colors, `fileRules`/`folderRules`, per-item icon maps |
63: | Enablement | `.obsidian/community-plugins.json` | Yes (already enabled in all vaults) |
64: | In-app icon picking | — | **No** — out of reach headlessly; edit rules instead |
65: 
66: ### Rulebook assets
67: 
68: | Asset | Contents | Use |
69: | --- | --- | --- |
70: | `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.full.json` | **Complete** automatic-rule payload: all 21 `fileRules` + 11 `folderRules` | Canonical copy/merge payload — the only authoritative full rule content |
71: | `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.full.md` | Template-conformant usage guide: rule-class coverage + merge contract | Usage companion for the payload; never a copy/merge source |
72: | `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.example.json` | Compact schema sample (2 file + 1 folder rules) | Schema reference only |
73: 
74: - The full asset contains **only the two mergeable rule arrays** — no `data.json` settings, no `dialogState`, no per-item override maps.
75: - It is **never a whole-`data.json` replacement**: merge it by stable rule `id` into a freshly-read vault `data.json` (update matching ids, append missing ids), preserving unrelated settings and user overrides.
76: 
77: ---
78: 
79: ## 5. RULE SHAPE (ONE RULE)
80: 
81: ```json
82: {
83:   "id": "FE8l6",
84:   "name": "Canvas boards",
85:   "icon": "lucide-layout-template",
86:   "color": "#8b5cf6",
87:   "match": "any",
88:   "conditions": [
89:     { "source": "extension", "operator": "is", "value": "canvas" }
90:   ],
91:   "enabled": true
92: }
93: ```
94: 
95: - `source`: `extension` (file rules) or `name` (folder rules).
96: - `operator`: `is` / `contains` (per the live vault rulebook).
97: - `match`: `any` (any condition matches) — `all` is supported by the schema.
98: - `icon`: `lucide-*` names; `color`: hex.
99: 
100: ---
101: 
102: ## 6. GOTCHAS
103: 
104: - **Backup before every write.** Take a `.bak` copy of `data.json` before merging (the bundle's `merge_rules.py` pattern: backup → merge → write).
105: - **Merge, never replace.** Preserve every setting and rule not being changed; user-customized rules stay untouched.
106: - **Full asset ≠ full `data.json`.** The canonical rule asset carries only the two rule arrays; applying it never touches settings, `dialogState`, or per-item overrides.
107: - **Never downgrade the plugin.** Only the rulebook is (re)applied.
108: - **Re-read `data.json` before operating** — the user may have changed icons in-app since the last read.
109: - Render confirmation needs an in-app reload; the file-layer claim is verified by JSON round-trip only.
110: 
111: ---
112: 
113: ## 7. RELATED RESOURCES
114: 
115: | File | Use it for |
116: | --- | --- |
117: | `data-model.md` | The full `data.json` contract: top-level keys, rulebook schema, visibility toggles, per-item icon maps, and safe-merge discipline |
118: | `workflows.md` | Safe recipes: add or edit rules, flip toggles, change colors, and merge the canonical rulebook |
119: | `troubleshooting.md` | Cause, detection, and recovery for invalid JSON, lost rules, missing icons, stale reads, and version drift |

15: # Iconic File-Layer Workflows
16: 
17: These recipes edit `.obsidian/plugins/iconic/data.json`. Every operation starts with a fresh read and a backup; every write is a merge, never a replace.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Change one Iconic rule or toggle and leave every other setting exactly as it was.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Adding, editing, disabling, or recoloring a rule.
30: - Flipping a visibility toggle.
31: - Applying the canonical rulebook to a vault.
32: 
33: ### Operating sequence
34: 
35: 1. Read `<vault>/.obsidian/plugins/iconic/data.json`.
36: 2. Back up: `cp data.json data.json.bak-$(date +%s)`.
37: 3. Apply the minimal merge (below).
38: 4. Write + re-parse JSON.
39: 5. Tell the user the icons render after an in-app reload.
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 2. RECIPES
44: 
45: ### Give an extension an icon (add a file rule)
46: 
47: - Append to `fileRules` (or edit the existing rule for that extension):
48: 
49: ```json
50: { "id": "gen<4chars>", "name": "PDF documents", "icon": "lucide-file-text", "color": "#ef4444", "match": "any", "conditions": [{ "source": "extension", "operator": "is", "value": "pdf" }], "enabled": true }
51: ```
52: 
53: - Prefer editing the existing rule when one matches the extension — merging beats duplicating.
54: 
55: ### Add a folder rule
56: 
57: - Append to `folderRules` with `source: name` conditions (`is` for exact names, `contains` for partial):
58: 
59: ```json
60: { "id": "gen<4chars>", "name": "Screenshots", "icon": "lucide-camera", "color": "#64748b", "match": "any", "conditions": [{ "source": "name", "operator": "is", "value": "screenshots" }], "enabled": true }
61: ```
62: 
63: ### Change a color
64: 
65: - Find the rule by `name` or `conditions.value`, set `color` to the new hex, keep `id` and everything else.
66: 
67: ### Disable/enable a rule
68: 
69: - Flip the rule's `enabled` boolean. Do not delete the rule unless asked.
70: 
71: ### Flip a visibility toggle
72: 
73: - e.g. `showAllFolderIcons` → `true` / `false`, or `showTagPillIcons`. Single-key merge.
74: 
75: ### Apply the canonical rulebook (bundle pattern)
76: 
77: - Same as the Iconic-Setup `merge_rules.py`: back up, then merge the canonical asset `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.full.json` into the freshly-read vault `data.json` — ONLY its `fileRules`/`folderRules` arrays (plus any explicitly requested keys).
78: - Merge by stable rule `id`: **update rules whose ids already exist, append rules with missing ids.** Preserve unrelated settings and user overrides (including per-item icon maps).
79: - The full asset contains only the two rule arrays — it is never a whole-`data.json` replacement. The compact `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.example.json` is schema reference only. Rule-class coverage and the merge contract are summarized in the usage companion `assets/plugins/iconic/iconic-rules.full.md`.
80: 
81: ---
82: 
83: ## 3. VERIFYING
84: 
85: - Re-parse the written JSON; confirm the changed rule/toggle reads back.
86: - Confirm no unrelated keys changed (diff against the backup).
87: - Rendering itself is in-app; state that the reload is the user's step.

16: # Obsidian MCP Tools Reference
17: 
18: - **MCP Server:** `obsidian`, the `obsidian-mcp-server` package (cyanheads) launched over **stdio** via `npx -y obsidian-mcp-server@latest`, registered as the `obsidian` manual in `.utcp_config.json`. It also supports Streamable HTTP on `127.0.0.1:3010/mcp`. On 2026-09-02 that `@latest` tag resolved to **v0.12.3**, so pin nothing to a version this document names.
19: - **Auth:** `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` (the Local REST API bearer token) plus `OBSIDIAN_BASE_URL` and `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_SSL`, interpolated into `.utcp_config.json`. The token comes from the Obsidian **Local REST API** plugin, not from an OAuth flow.
20: - **Invocation:** Code Mode `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })` via `mcp__code_mode__call_tool_chain` — a single TypeScript code string with direct access to registered tools as hierarchical functions (not an array of `{tool, input}` records).
21: - **Tool naming:** Code Mode namespaces every registered tool as `<manual_name>.<manual_name>_<tool_name>` — one dot then underscore. For this manual the pattern is `obsidian.obsidian_<tool_name>` (e.g. `obsidian.obsidian_get_note`). Do not guess a tool name — confirm every one with `tool_info()`/`list_tools()` before calling.
22: 
23: > **App-backed surface:** unlike `notesmd-cli` (headless, filesystem), this MCP server drives the vault through Obsidian's **Local REST API plugin**, which requires a **running Obsidian app**. If no app/token is available, route to the `notesmd-cli` CLI instead (see `obsidian-cli-commands.md`).
24: 
25: > **Verification status:** the server builds **14 tools** and exposes **12**. `obsidian_list_commands` and `obsidian_execute_command` are withheld while `enableCommands` is false, and calling either returns a JSON-RPC `-32602 Tool not found`. All twelve exposed tools were enumerated and exercised against a live vault on 2026-09-02, in [`cli-versus-mcp.md`](cli-versus-mcp.md). Reconfirm with a fresh `list_tools()` before relying on a signature, since the pinned `@latest` tag moves.
26: 
27: ---

29: ## 1. OVERVIEW
30: 
31: The Obsidian MCP server is the app-backed surface in mcp-obsidian, used when you want to operate a **running** vault through the Local REST API rather than the filesystem. Confirmed capabilities: read a note, write a note, search notes, manage tags, and delete a note.
32: 
33: Use this reference when:
34: - Routing a request to MCP (not the CLI) because a live app + Local REST API is available — see the router in `../ROUTER.md` §3 MACHINE ROUTER
35: - Writing Code Mode `call_tool_chain({ code: "..." })` invocations
36: - Confirming whether a capability is supported before routing to it (enumerate with `list_tools()`)
37: 
38: ---

40: ## 2. PREREQUISITES
41: 
42: - Code Mode MCP configured, with the `obsidian` manual in `.utcp_config.json` (not `opencode.json`, `.mcp.json`, or `claude_desktop_config.json` — those are for native/non-Code-Mode MCP tools)
43: - Obsidian **Local REST API plugin v4.0.0+** installed and enabled in the vault
44: - A **running Obsidian app** with that vault open (the server talks to the app, not the disk)
45: - `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` set to the Local REST API bearer token; `OBSIDIAN_BASE_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:27123`) and `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_SSL` (default `false`) available to Code Mode
46: - Node.js 18+ and npx available (the manual launches `obsidian-mcp-server@latest` on demand via `npx -y`)
47: - AI client restarted after config change
48: 
49: > **Registration note:** the `obsidian` manual is already registered in `.utcp_config.json` — this document describes that wiring but does not modify it.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 3. AUTHENTICATION
54: 
55: `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` is the bearer token issued by the Obsidian **Local REST API** plugin (Settings → Local REST API → copy the API key). It is interpolated into `.utcp_config.json` for the `obsidian` manual as `${obsidian_OBSIDIAN_API_KEY}`. There is no OAuth flow and no browser authorization step.
56:

59: | `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` | — (required) | Local REST API bearer token |
60: | `OBSIDIAN_BASE_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:27123` | Local REST API endpoint |

=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/notion-migration.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Finish a Notion migration at the file layer and prove parity before the source workspace is retired.

### When to Use

Open it once `mcp-notion`'s inventory exists and the Importer has run, or before either, to see what the import will leave behind.

A flawless migration is not a single tool run. The **Obsidian Importer's Notion API mode** is the only import path that preserves database structure — it converts blocks to Markdown, generates `.base` files for databases, and resolves cross-page references through a three-phase placeholder system (Import → Resolution, up to 10 rounds → Cleanup). It runs once, in the Obsidian desktop app, driven by a human. Everything after that import — verifying what the importer converted, rebuilding what it dropped, and proving parity — is an agent task performed at the file layer against the vault the importer produced.

The importer auto-converts:

- Pages and nested hierarchy
- Internal links
- Databases → Bases
- Properties → frontmatter
- Formulas and rollups → Bases formulas (a hybrid strategy)
- Single relations → wikilinks
- Block attachments
- Page covers

It does **not** convert:

- Comments
- Secondary database views
- Two-way relation back-references
- Gallery cover images
- External attachments (unless opted in)
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/obsidian-cli-commands.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Run the right vault command against the right profile, with the flags and failure behavior that profile actually has.

### When to Use

- Choosing between `notesmd-cli` and the official `obsidian` CLI for a task.
- Looking up a vault command, flag, or agent invariant before scripting one.

`notesmd-cli` is a Go CLI that reads and writes the vault's markdown files directly. Because it never talks to a running app, it is the reliable surface for scripted, headless agent workflows: create notes, search content, list files, edit frontmatter, and manage which vault is the default — all against the filesystem.

The official `obsidian` CLI is a thin remote control shipped inside the desktop app (GA in desktop v1.12.4, Feb 2026). It drives an app that is **already running** and does not start one. It is the right surface when you need the live app's resolved link graph, its computed tag/task index, its plugins, sync and file history, or its rendering. Agent-facing usage, preflight and the exit-0 failure contract: [`official-cli-agent-usage.md`](official-cli-agent-usage.md).

**Key agent advantages of `notesmd-cli`:**
- No app dependency — runs on servers, in CI, over SSH
- Operates on plain files — deterministic, greppable, diff-able
- Multi-vault aware — `add-vault` / `set-default-vault` route commands to the right vault

> The binary is named `notesmd-cli` (renamed from "obsidian-cli" to avoid confusion with the official CLI). Do not invoke it as `obsidian-cli`.

---

## 2. PREREQUISITES
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/official-cli-agent-usage.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Make the app-backed CLI safe to script: prove it will answer, read its stdout instead of its exit status, and never let the human's open note become the target.

### When to Use

- Scripting the official `obsidian` CLI against a running app.
- Diagnosing a preflight failure or an exit-0 error.

### Registration

The official CLI ships inside the Obsidian desktop app and is registered from Settings → General → Command line interface → Register CLI. On macOS that registration creates a symlink at `/usr/local/bin/obsidian` pointing into the app bundle.

Three properties decide how an agent must use it, and all three differ from an ordinary UNIX tool:

1. **It answers only while the desktop app is running.** With the app down, every invocation fails immediately.
2. **It reports in-app failures with exit status 0.** Branching on `$?` treats a missing file, an unknown command and an unknown vault as success.
3. **It defaults to the note the human currently has open** when no target is given, including for mutating commands.

Use `notesmd-cli` for file-shaped work. Reach for this CLI when the outcome needs the live app: its resolved link graph, its plugins, its sync history, or its rendering.

---

=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/plugins/health-md/troubleshooting.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Name the one cause behind a Health.md failure before changing a file or a setting.

### When to Use

- A Health.md chart is empty, missing, or shows data the user did not export.
- A data file is ignored, misread, or silently best-effort.
- The cause could sit in the folder, pattern, format, schema, platform, or render block.

| Symptom | Most likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| "No data found" in the chart | Data folder path or file pattern setting doesn't cover the files |
| Chart shows bundled example data | Data folder missing or empty — plugin falls back to deterministic bundled example data; verify against an authentic source file |
| Chart renders but is empty | No records, denied permission, disabled export selection, absent platform capability, or unsupported visualization |
| Files ignored | Format mismatch (`auto` misdetect), or a schema version the installed build does not read (current exporter: daily v8 / roll-up v9; plugin v2.1.0 ceiling is VERIFY — historically v7) |
| Wrong numbers | Roll-up duplicates daily records, or mixed timezone contexts |
| Platform-specific surface missing | iOS-only feature on Android, or a known Android gap (see §3) |
| Plugin settings lost | `data.json` edited into invalid JSON |

---

## 2. DIAGNOSIS SEQUENCE

=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/themes/theme-development.md

### When to Use

- Building a theme from the official sample.
- Checking the two required files or the `manifest.json` name rule.
- Preparing a theme for submission to the community catalog.

A theme is a folder under `.obsidian/themes/` containing two required files:

```
.obsidian/themes/<ThemeName>/
├── manifest.json
└── theme.css
```

- `manifest.json` — metadata. Its `name` field **MUST equal the theme directory name**.
- `theme.css` — the **entire stylesheet**. One file holds the whole theme; there is no partials split.

There is no `main.js`, no commands, no settings — a theme is styling only. Behavioral changes belong to a plugin (see `plugin-development.md`).

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

A theme is a **full restyle of Obsidian's appearance** shipped as a single `theme.css` plus a `manifest.json`. It is one of three extension surfaces.

### When to Use

- Installing, activating, or managing a community theme.
- Checking which theme is active from the file layer.
- Distinguishing a theme from a snippet or a plugin.

The three extension surfaces are distinct:

| Surface | What it changes | Carrier file | Lives in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Theme** | Look only (colors, spacing, typography) | `theme.css` | `.obsidian/themes/<ThemeName>/` |
| **Snippet** | Small targeted CSS overrides | a `.css` file | `.obsidian/snippets/` |
| **Plugin** | Behavior / logic (commands, views, settings) | `main.js` | `.obsidian/plugins/<plugin-id>/` |

A theme restyles; a snippet overrides; a plugin adds behavior. A theme package has **no `main.js` and no commands** — it cannot change what Obsidian does, only how it looks.

=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/troubleshooting.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

An Obsidian failure reaches the fix for the surface that produced it, whether that is the headless CLI, the official app-backed CLI, or the MCP server.

### When to Use

- A `notesmd-cli` or `obsidian` command fails or is not found.
- An MCP call returns 401, connection refused, or an npx launch error.
- A search returns nothing and you need to confirm that is the real answer.
- A task keeps failing because the app is not running.

Most failures fall into six categories:
1. **Installation / PATH** — `notesmd-cli` or `obsidian` not on PATH (often a GUI-vs-shell PATH mismatch).
2. **Official CLI not registered** — the `obsidian` binary was never enabled in Settings.
3. **Official CLI registered but the app is down** — the most common official-CLI failure, and the only one that exits non-zero (§5b).
4. **Local REST API prerequisite** — the plugin is not enabled, or is on the wrong port / SSL mode.
5. **Authentication** — `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` unset or wrong.
6. **MCP launch** — npx cannot fetch `obsidian-mcp-server`, or the app is not running.

Start with the Quick Diagnostics sequence (§3) before diving into specifics.

=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/cli-versus-mcp.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

This reference answers one question: given a running Obsidian app, which of the two surfaces should an agent drive, and when should it switch. Section 2 records the machine and vault the numbers came from. Sections 3 and 4 hold the per-capability results in each app state, Section 5 the timings, Section 6 the rule that follows, and Section 7 what stayed unproven.

### Verdict

**Default to the official `obsidian` CLI, wrapped in a stdout error check.** Reach for the MCP server only for section-scoped editing, tag-list management, or a batch of more than roughly twenty calls, and only after confirming the Local REST API plugin is enabled.

Three measurements decided it.

| What decided it | The CLI | The MCP server |
|---|---|---|
| **Prerequisites** | The running app, nothing else | The running app **plus** an enabled Local REST API plugin, a bearer token, Node and `npx` |
| **Surface size** | 106 commands | 12 tools |
| **Worked on this machine as configured** | Yes | **No**. The plugin was installed but disabled, so every vault call failed |

The MCP server is better designed for an agent. It gives typed errors, a mandatory explicit target, and a create that refuses collisions. It still loses on the two things that decide a default: it does less, and it was not switched on. Section 6 states the rule that follows.

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Finish a Notion migration at the file layer and prove parity before the source workspace is retired.

### When to Use

Open it once `mcp-notion`'s inventory exists and the Importer has run, or before either, to see what the import will leave behind.

A flawless migration is not a single tool run. The **Obsidian Importer's Notion API mode** is the only import path that preserves database structure — it converts blocks to Markdown, generates `.base` files for databases, and resolves cross-page references through a three-phase placeholder system (Import → Resolution, up to 10 rounds → Cleanup). It runs once, in the Obsidian desktop app, driven by a human. Everything after that import — verifying what the importer converted, rebuilding what it dropped, and proving parity — is an agent task performed at the file layer against the vault the importer produced.

The importer auto-converts:

- Pages and nested hierarchy
- Internal links
- Databases → Bases
- Properties → frontmatter
- Formulas and rollups → Bases formulas (a hybrid strategy)
- Single relations → wikilinks
- Block attachments
- Page covers

It does **not** convert:

- Comments
- Secondary database views
- Two-way relation back-references
- Gallery cover images
- External attachments (unless opted in)
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/obsidian-cli-commands.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Run the right vault command against the right profile, with the flags and failure behavior that profile actually has.

### When to Use

- Choosing between `notesmd-cli` and the official `obsidian` CLI for a task.
- Looking up a vault command, flag, or agent invariant before scripting one.

`notesmd-cli` is a Go CLI that reads and writes the vault's markdown files directly. Because it never talks to a running app, it is the reliable surface for scripted, headless agent workflows: create notes, search content, list files, edit frontmatter, and manage which vault is the default — all against the filesystem.

The official `obsidian` CLI is a thin remote control shipped inside the desktop app (GA in desktop v1.12.4, Feb 2026). It drives an app that is **already running** and does not start one. It is the right surface when you need the live app's resolved link graph, its computed tag/task index, its plugins, sync and file history, or its rendering. Agent-facing usage, preflight and the exit-0 failure contract: [`official-cli-agent-usage.md`](official-cli-agent-usage.md).

**Key agent advantages of `notesmd-cli`:**
- No app dependency — runs on servers, in CI, over SSH
- Operates on plain files — deterministic, greppable, diff-able
- Multi-vault aware — `add-vault` / `set-default-vault` route commands to the right vault

> The binary is named `notesmd-cli` (renamed from "obsidian-cli" to avoid confusion with the official CLI). Do not invoke it as `obsidian-cli`.

=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/official-cli-agent-usage.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Make the app-backed CLI safe to script: prove it will answer, read its stdout instead of its exit status, and never let the human's open note become the target.

### When to Use

- Scripting the official `obsidian` CLI against a running app.
- Diagnosing a preflight failure or an exit-0 error.

### Registration

The official CLI ships inside the Obsidian desktop app and is registered from Settings → General → Command line interface → Register CLI. On macOS that registration creates a symlink at `/usr/local/bin/obsidian` pointing into the app bundle.

Three properties decide how an agent must use it, and all three differ from an ordinary UNIX tool:

1. **It answers only while the desktop app is running.** With the app down, every invocation fails immediately.
2. **It reports in-app failures with exit status 0.** Branching on `$?` treats a missing file, an unknown command and an unknown vault as success.
3. **It defaults to the note the human currently has open** when no target is given, including for mutating commands.

Use `notesmd-cli` for file-shaped work. Reach for this CLI when the outcome needs the live app: its resolved link graph, its plugins, its sync history, or its rendering.

- Placing or checking a `health-viz` block.
- Proving a chart is fed by authentic data.

### Operating sequence

1. Read the plugin settings (`.obsidian/plugins/health-md/data.json`) and resolve the **actual selected data folder**, structure, pattern, and format — never assume the default.
2. Inspect what exists: files, formats, schema versions, roll-ups, dictionary, entry notes.
3. Write/append data files using an existing authentic file's shape as the template.
4. Place/adjust the `health-viz` render block in the target note.
5. Verify the file layer by reading the files back — the visual itself renders in-app only.

=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/plugins/iconic/troubleshooting.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

### When to Use

- Icons are missing, wrong, or the wrong color.
- The plugin will not load after a write.
- Rules vanished after an edit, or an unknown key appeared after an update.

| Symptom | Most likely cause |
|---|---|
| No icons at all | `showAllFileIcons`/`showAllFolderIcons` off, plugin disabled, or app not reloaded |
| One file/folder has no icon | No rule matches (extension/name not covered) or its rule is `enabled: false` |
| Icon renders but wrong color | Rule color edited elsewhere, or a per-item override (`fileIcons`) shadows the rule |
| Plugin won't load | `data.json` invalid JSON (bad merge) |
| Rules missing after an edit | A replace-style write overwrote the user's rulebook |
| Unknown keys after update | Plugin version newer than 1.1.10 added settings |

The vault has **24 community plugins** enabled (`.obsidian/community-plugins.json`). They split into three operating classes, and the counts add up: **2 documented + 13 undocumented file-layer + 9 UI/automatic = 24**.

### Purpose

`plugin-operation-logic.md` ships in the `mcp-obsidian` mode at `references/plugins/` and defines one operating model for every plugin the mode covers: locate the plugin's persisted data, edit the data directly, and let the app re-render. ## 2. WHERE PLUGINS KEEP THEIR DATA
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/themes/customization.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Keep every visual change in a snippet the user can toggle off, while the theme underneath stays updatable.

### When to Use

- A user wants a visual change to an installed theme.
- Deciding between a CSS snippet and a variable override.
- Checking whether a snippet is actually enabled.

There are two customization levers, both file-based:

| Lever | What it does | Carrier | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **CSS snippet** | Small targeted CSS override | a `.css` file | `.obsidian/snippets/` |
| **CSS variable override** | Restyle a design token (color, spacing, typography) | inside a snippet or theme | same `.css` file |

Snippets are the safe customization surface. A snippet overrides specific rules; the theme underneath stays intact and can still be updated without losing your changes.

## 2. CSS SNIPPETS
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/themes/plugin-development.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Choose the right build surface (theme, snippet, or plugin) and know the package a plugin needs before writing code.

### When to Use

- A need is behavioral rather than visual, and a theme or snippet will not cover it.
- Checking the required plugin files, manifest fields, or the sample starting point.
- Preparing a plugin for community submission.

| Surface | What it changes | Carrier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Theme** | Look only | `theme.css` |
| **Snippet** | Small CSS overrides | a `.css` file |
| **Plugin** | Behavior / logic (commands, views, settings) | `main.js` |

A plugin adds behavior a theme cannot: commands, custom views, workspace actions, persisted settings. If a need is purely visual, use a theme or snippet instead.

### Boundaries

This document is deliberately an **overview**. For depth on the Plugin API, build tooling, lifecycle hooks, settings UI, and publishing, read `docs.obsidian.md/Plugins`. The `mcp-obsidian` mode interacts with installed plugins at the file layer (manifest, `data.json` settings, enablement in `community-plugins.json`); authoring and compiling a plugin is out of scope for the mode.

## 2. PLUGIN ANATOMY
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/themes/theme-development.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

Produce a theme package Obsidian loads, that works in both dark and light modes, and that the community catalog accepts.

### When to Use

- Building a theme from the official sample.
- Checking the two required files or the `manifest.json` name rule.
- Preparing a theme for submission to the community catalog.

A theme is a folder under `.obsidian/themes/` containing two required files:

```
.obsidian/themes/<ThemeName>/
├── manifest.json
└── theme.css
```

- `manifest.json` — metadata. Its `name` field **MUST equal the theme directory name**.
- `theme.css` — the **entire stylesheet**. One file holds the whole theme; there is no partials split.

There is no `main.js`, no commands, no settings — a theme is styling only. Behavioral changes belong to a plugin (see `plugin-development.md`).

---

## 2. THE SAMPLE THEME STARTING POINT
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/themes/themes.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

A theme is a **full restyle of Obsidian's appearance** shipped as a single `theme.css` plus a `manifest.json`. It is one of three extension surfaces.

### When to Use

- Installing, activating, or managing a community theme.
- Checking which theme is active from the file layer.
- Distinguishing a theme from a snippet or a plugin.

The three extension surfaces are distinct:

| Surface | What it changes | Carrier file | Lives in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Theme** | Look only (colors, spacing, typography) | `theme.css` | `.obsidian/themes/<ThemeName>/` |
| **Snippet** | Small targeted CSS overrides | a `.css` file | `.obsidian/snippets/` |
| **Plugin** | Behavior / logic (commands, views, settings) | `main.js` | `.obsidian/plugins/<plugin-id>/` |

A theme restyles; a snippet overrides; a plugin adds behavior. A theme package has **no `main.js` and no commands** — it cannot change what Obsidian does, only how it looks.

## 2. BASE COLOR SCHEME VS COMMUNITY THEME
=== .skilled/skills/mcp-tooling/mcp-obsidian/references/troubleshooting.md
## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

An Obsidian failure reaches the fix for the surface that produced it, whether that is the headless CLI, the official app-backed CLI, or the MCP server.

### When to Use

- A `notesmd-cli` or `obsidian` command fails or is not found.
- An MCP call returns 401, connection refused, or an npx launch error.
- A search returns nothing and you need to confirm that is the real answer.
- A task keeps failing because the app is not running.

Most failures fall into six categories:
1. **Installation / PATH** — `notesmd-cli` or `obsidian` not on PATH (often a GUI-vs-shell PATH mismatch).
2. **Official CLI not registered** — the `obsidian` binary was never enabled in Settings.
3. **Official CLI registered but the app is down** — the most common official-CLI failure, and the only one that exits non-zero (§5b).
4. **Local REST API prerequisite** — the plugin is not enabled, or is on the wrong port / SSL mode.
5. **Authentication** — `OBSIDIAN_API_KEY` unset or wrong.
6. **MCP launch** — npx cannot fetch `obsidian-mcp-server`, or the app is not running.

Start with the Quick Diagnostics sequence (§3) before diving into specifics.

changelog/v0.19.0.0.md:20:Phase 003 authored the Notion Bases reference tree before the plugin was installed anywhere, so its schema examples were correctly marked `VERIFY`. The operator's vault installation at v1.12.0 surfaced the plugin's README, which confirmed most of those facts, exposed the `nb-database` embed syntax and corrected the rollup keyword from `average` to `avg`.
changelog/v0.19.0.0.md:31:- **The Dataview tree and Phase 003 deliverables stay unchanged.** The `references/plugins/dataview/*` tree was not edited, and the Notion Bases Dataview-supplement section still points to it without duplicating its content. `feature-catalog/plugins/notion-bases.md` and the `OBS-022` manual-testing scenario remain as-is.
feature-catalog/plugins/health-md.md:18:Health.md Visualizations (repo `codybontecou/health-md-visualizations`, installed v2.1.0 in every vault by Phase 11) renders Apple Health and Android Health exports from plain data files in a vault folder (default `Health/`). The mode operates the **data files**, never the chart UI. Formats: JSON (`healthmd.health_data` daily schema through v8), CSV, Markdown frontmatter (Bases-style), Obsidian Bases; roll-ups are `healthmd.rollup_summary` v9. Compatibility profiles: Apple current export daily v8 / roll-up v9 (whether installed plugin v2.1.0 reads v8/v9 is VERIFY — historically v0–v7), Android frozen v4, and Android analytical v5 — format names are shared, but version and semantic differences stay explicit. Chart coverage is shared across platforms for common activity, heart, respiratory/vitals, sleep, mobility, workout, body, nutrition, and hearing fields; Mood/State of Mind and HealthKit-style medication events are iOS-only; Android walking symmetry is partial and Android Stand can use an explicit steps-derived proxy when `standHours` is missing. Roll-ups live under `Health/Rollups/`; `_healthmd_data_dictionary.json` holds canonical metric ids/units. The plugin watches the folder and refreshes its cache on file changes. A `health-viz` block's `type` must be a registered renderer (43 documented across 18 categories — catalog in `references/plugins/health-md/health-md.md` §4). Beyond the plugin, the companion app (`healthmd.app`) can merge metrics into Obsidian daily-note frontmatter and ships a `healthmd` CLI and a `healthmd-mcp` MCP server (21 tools reading iPhone HealthKit via a Mac loopback) — separate from this plugin; see `references/plugins/health-md/health-md.md` §7.
changelog/v0.4.0.0.md:17:- **`references/plugins/health-md/` is the new Health.md Visualizations (`health-md`) reference set.** It covers Apple Health export data files (JSON/CSV/Markdown/Bases) in the vault data folder (default `Health/`), schema v0–v7, roll-ups under `Health/Rollups/`, `_healthmd_data_dictionary.json`, render-block placement and the hard rule to never fabricate health data. Health.md Visualizations was installed and enabled in all three vaults (packet Phase 11).

14: # mcp-obsidian Router
15: 
16: The machine router for [`SKILL.md`](./SKILL.md). `SKILL.md` keeps the short routing prose and the
17: link that points here; this file holds the declaration a reader parses to decide what loads.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: An Obsidian vault or note request reaches this skill when it names Obsidian, a vault, `notesmd-cli`, the cyanheads MCP, the official app-backed `obsidian` CLI, or one of the two documented plugins, and the `mcp-tooling` hub's `mcp-obsidian` mode signal selects the packet. From there the router selects among the CLI command references, the official-CLI agent-usage guide, the cyanheads MCP tool catalog, the troubleshooting and Notion-migration guides, and the plugin and theme families under `references/plugins/` and `references/themes/`. `references/obsidian-cli-commands.md` is the declared default, offered as a fallback suggestion rather than loaded by any scored route.
24: 
25: The router answers one question: given a request, which skill-local resources load, in what order, and
26: what happens when nothing matches. Every path below stays inside this skill folder, and no resource
27: loads before an intent selects it.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. INTENT MODEL
32:
